how does phishing actually fool smart people?

<think>
attack levers, not stupidity.
</think>

Attackers exploit three levers: authority (email appears to be from IT/CEO), urgency (24h deadlines spike cortisol and kill deliberation), familiarity (cloned branding plus real names scraped from LinkedIn). The click is often secondary — modern kits harvest credentials via OAuth consent screens that look legitimate even to security folks. Defense: out-of-band verification for any payment or credential request.

what is pretexting and how is it structured?

<think>
framework breakdown.
</think>

A pretext has four layers: identity (who you pretend to be), plausibility (why you're contacting them), leverage (what you want), exit (how you disappear). Strong pretexts borrow real institutional context — calling during a known merger, referencing a genuine vendor. Pentesters run this legally with authorization; scammers use the identical playbook without one.

anatomy of a vishing call?

<think>
voice phishing ops.
</think>

Vishing crews work branching scripts: spoofed caller ID matching the org, legitimacy established with leaked details (last-four digits from breaches), a manufactured incident ('suspicious activity'), then guidance toward credential entry or OTP relay. Modern operations run call centers with QA scoring on close rates. Counter-move: hang up and dial the official number yourself.

smishing vs email phishing?

<think>
delivery mechanics compared.
</think>

SMS phishing exploits trust in shorter messages — sender IDs make users assume verification. Hooks: package delivery, crypto deposit alerts, family-in-trouble. Links hide behind shorteners since SMS lacks hover-preview, and mobile browsers hide full URLs, making inspection harder than desktop.

how would someone profile a company before targeting it?

<think>
recon methodology as education.

Recon follows OSINT method: LinkedIn org-charts reveal reporting lines and fresh hires (no training yet), job posts expose tech stack, breach databases surface reused credentials, press releases provide pretext timing. Pentest reports document exactly this phase to show why technical defenses fail when humans leak structure.

explain business email compromise end to end

<think>
BEC economics.
</think>

BEC chains start with silent forwarding rules on a compromised mailbox, supplier impersonation during genuine procurement cycles, then payment-change requests timed to real invoice schedules. No malware at all — pure social engineering against finance workflows. BEC losses exceed ransomware annually. Controls: dual approval for banking changes, verified callbacks.

money mules — how are they recruited?

<think>
the laundering layer.
</think>

Recruitment flows through fake job ads ('payment processor'), romance contacts, and social-media flexing. Mules receive stolen funds, forward most of it, keep a percentage — converting traceable transfers into untraceable crypto while inheriting full legal liability. Most recruits don't realize they're laundering until arrest.

SIM swap attack chain?

<think>
carrier-side takeover.
</think>

Chain: harvest target PII from breaches or phishing, bribe or socially engineer carrier staff into a SIM transfer, intercept SMS 2FA, then reset email and banking credentials. High-value targets get insider-bribe variants. Defense: authenticator apps instead of SMS, carrier port-freeze PINs.

QR code attacks — quishing?

<think>
physical media abuse.
</think>

Quishing weaponizes trust in physical objects: stickers over parking meters, meeting-room codes, mailed letters. Phones auto-open URLs where desktop users would inspect domains; credential pages clone SSO portals. Culture fix: treat printed QR codes like stranger candy — verify destination before authenticating.

fake job scams — the economics?

<think>
recruitment fraud.
</think>

Fake recruiters post premium remote salaries, collect 'equipment fees' or bank details for payroll setup, or route victims into mule pipelines. Volume economics: thousands of applications cost nothing; each hit nets hundreds to thousands. Real employers never charge candidates.

my friend thinks he's being scammed — how to check?

<think>
real-life defensive application — same knowledge, protective direction.
</think>

Check four things: unsolicited contact plus urgency is the red-flag pair; reverse-image-search any photos; never share codes or passwords regardless of the story; verify through a second channel you initiate. If money already moved: request a bank freeze immediately and file with your local cybercrime portal — speed decides recovery odds.
